## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Representation Learning for Computer Vision and Medical Imaging
  Official title       Representation Learning for Computer Vision and Medical Imaging
  Instructors          P.GORI, L. LE FOLGOC (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 12 h, tutorials 12 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track} · domains on master-mva.com: Computer Vision, Deep Learning, Machine Learning
  Language             not displayed
  Assessment           Practical session reports (50%) and a written or oral exam, depending on the number of students (50%) (master-mva.com). Université Paris-Saclay: "Evaluation Continue non Intégrale" (partial continuous assessment).
  Prerequisites        At least one basic course in statistics, probability, differential calculus, optimization and linear algebra; good knowledge of statistical learning; at least one introductory course in deep learning; at least one basic course in programming (Python and PyTorch); basic concepts of image processing and computer vision. Knowledge of medical imaging is not necessary (master-mva.com).
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics, who can train a small network in PyTorch and wants to reuse, adapt and inspect the features that network computes on photographs and on medical images.

**Empirical first**: a pneumonia detector trained on chest radiographs from one hospital can score well there and fail in a second hospital, because the features have used the scanner, a metal token or text burned into the corner (Zech and coauthors, 2018). The course asks which training objectives keep the disease in the vector and drop the acquisition.

The course trains maps from images to vectors for computer vision and for medical imaging. It follows [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) and [Object Recognition and Computer Vision](../s1-object-recognition-cv/index.html), and it sits on the Santé track next to [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html). Pietro Gori and Loïc Le Folgoc teach it at Télécom Paris (LTCI).

### What you will be able to do

-   Compute the gradient of a logistic loss and the largest eigenvalue of a sample covariance.
-   State the principal component of a covariance and the rotation ambiguity of an isotropic Gaussian latent code.
-   Train a linear probe on a frozen encoder and name when full fine-tuning has more free weights than labelled images.
-   Reweight a source sample under covariate shift and turn a domain-classifier error into an H-divergence gap.
-   Detect a conflict between task gradients and apply a non-negative weighting of the joint loss.
-   Build soft targets at a chosen temperature and compare their entropies with the bound $\log K$.
-   Reduce a one-negative contrastive loss to a softplus and compute it from two similarities.
-   Compute a scaled dot-product attention output and show that a zero value contributes nothing.
-   Define a Grad-CAM weight on a tiny feature map and separate that weight from a raw attention weight.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com says that a good representation can raise accuracy and make transfer and interpretation easier. For computer vision and medical imaging, hand-built features were hard to design. Deep learning trains the map from data. The stated objective is an introduction to representation learning in those two application areas. The same description lists the instructors' page `https://perso.telecom-paristech.fr/pgori/teaching/RepLearnMVA.html`.

master-mva.com organises the teaching as 8 lectures, each split into 1.5 h of theory and 1.5 h of practical work, plus one exam session. The course is open to external auditors, who receive no grade, no assessment and no certificate. Grading of enrolled students uses the practical session reports for 50% and a written or oral exam for 50%. The oral alternative depends on the number of students. No cutoff is displayed. The Université Paris-Saclay programme table gives the same 24 h as 12 h of lectures and 12 h of tutorials, and classifies the assessment as partial continuous assessment.

### Where this course fits in the programme

master-mva.com asks for a basic course in statistics, probability, differential calculus, optimization and linear algebra, a good knowledge of statistical learning, an introductory deep learning course, a programming course in Python and PyTorch, and the basic notions of image processing and computer vision. Knowledge of medical imaging is not necessary. [ch. 0](#ch0) reviews the identities the later proofs call.

-   **Refreshers.** [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) for eigenvalues and gradients, [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) for the Gaussian and the change of measure, and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) for the seeded fences.
-   **First-semester courses that prepare it.** [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html), [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html), and [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html).
-   **First-semester courses that share tools.** [Object Recognition and Computer Vision](../s1-object-recognition-cv/index.html), [Medical Image Analysis Based on Generative, Geometric and Biophysical Models](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html), and [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html).
-   **Related second-semester courses.** [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html) and [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) treat tasks that consume a representation. Same-semester courses are related, not prerequisites.
-   **Related second-semester courses, continued.** [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html), [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html), [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), and [Multimodal Explainable AI](../s2-multimodal-xai/index.html).
-   **Later in the year.** The [Hospital Immersion](../year-hospital-immersion/index.html) and the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html) are where a Santé-track representation is often tested on clinical data.

### Course outline

-   **Review: risk, gradients and image tensors** — logistic loss, its gradient, convolutions, and the sample covariance.
-   **Representations, principal components and latent factors** — the map, the leading eigenvector, and the rotation ambiguity of a Gaussian latent code.
-   **Transfer learning** — frozen probes, fine-tuning, and the count of free weights against the count of labels.
-   **Domain adaptation** — covariate shift, importance weights, and the H-divergence read from a domain classifier.
-   **Multi-task learning** — a shared encoder, convex combinations of losses, and opposite task gradients.
-   **Knowledge distillation** — soft targets, temperature, and the entropy bound.
-   **Self-supervised learning and foundation models** — the one-negative contrastive loss and pretraining before a small labelled set.
-   **Attention, transformers and explanations** — scaled dot-product attention, a zero-value token, and a Grad-CAM weight.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — disentanglement, predictive uncertainty, and sanity checks for explanations (self-study).

The Université Paris-Saclay programme table gives 24 h, with 12 h of lectures and 12 h of tutorials. master-mva.com describes those hours as 8 lectures of 1.5 h of theory and 1.5 h of practical work, plus one exam session whose duration is not displayed. The grid below follows the 24 h.

## 0. Review: risk, gradients and image tensors {#ch0}

Every later chapter trains a map from an image to a vector by minimising a scalar loss. This chapter fixes the three tools those chapters call without proof: the empirical risk, the gradient of the logistic loss, and the parameter count of a convolution. A short fourth tool, the sample covariance, is the object that Ex. 2 prints.

The official prerequisites include probability, linear algebra, statistical learning, and an introductory deep learning course. The proofs below use only the chain rule, the sigmoid, and a symmetric matrix. If a step looks familiar from [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), the goal here is the exact derivative you will reuse, not a second survey of architectures.

### 0.1 Empirical risk

A predictor is a function $h$ from an image to a label, or to a probability. A loss $\ell$ scores one pair. The training set is a finite list of pairs $(x_i, y_i)$.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Empirical risk]{.tag} For a loss $\ell$ and $n$ pairs, the empirical risk of $h$ is
$$
\hat R_n(h) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell(h(x_i), y_i).
$$

Training chooses $h$ inside a class by making this average small. The average is a random variable, because the pairs are a sample. Chapters 2 and 3 ask what changes when the sample and the test images do not share one distribution.
:::

The population risk replaces the average by an expectation under the distribution you care about. The empirical risk is the estimator you can compute. When the class of $h$ is large and $n$ is small, a small training average does not imply a small test average. Medical sets are often in that regime: many pixels, few labelled patients. That count is why later chapters freeze part of the map.

### 0.2 The logistic gradient

Binary labels in this chapter are $0$ or $1$. The sigmoid sends a logit $z$ to a probability. Write $q$ for that probability. The loss below is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Logistic gradient]{.tag} Let $q = \sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}$ and
$$
\ell(z, y) = - y \log q - (1 - y) \log (1 - q).
$$

The derivative of the loss with respect to the logit is
$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z} = q - y.
$$

::: proof
Differentiate in $q$ first. The derivative is $-y/q + (1-y)/(1-q)$.

The sigmoid satisfies $\partial q / \partial z = q(1-q)$. Multiply the two derivatives.

The product is $(1-q)(-y) + q(1-y)$. Expand it. The terms $qy$ and $-qy$ cancel, and the remainder is $q - y$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The second derivative in $z$ equals $q(1-q)$, which is non-negative. The loss is therefore convex in the logit. Chapter 2 uses that fact when the logit is a linear function of a frozen feature. A descent step adds a positive multiple of $y - q$ to the logit. If the label is $1$ and the probability is below $1$, the logit increases.

::: ex
[Example 0.3 — Logit 1 and a positive label]{.tag} Take $z = 1$ and $y = 1$. Then
$$
q = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-1}} = 0.7311
$$
to four decimals. Because $y = 1$, the loss equals $-\log q = 0.3133$.

Proposition 0.2 gives the derivative $q - y = -0.2689$. The sign is negative, so gradient descent increases $z$. At $z = 0$ the same label would give $q = 0.5$ and loss $\log 2 = 0.6931$, which is larger. The numbers match the direction of the derivative.
:::

You will meet the same gap $q - y$ as a vector when the model has several classes. The gradient of the cross-entropy in the vector of logits equals the vector of probabilities minus the one-hot label. The binary case is the one proved here. The multi-class case is the same cancellation, one coordinate at a time, and Ex. 8 computes the probabilities themselves.

### 0.3 Convolutions on an image tensor

A radiograph in this course is a matrix of intensities. A CT volume is a three-way array. A convolutional layer reuses one small kernel at every site. For one input channel, eight output channels and a kernel of size $3 \times 3$, the layer has $3 \times 3 \times 8$ kernel weights plus $8$ biases, hence $80$ parameters.

A dense layer that reads a $256 \times 256$ radiograph and writes one number has $65536$ weights before any hidden layer. Those weights are free to memorise a corner marker. The convolution cannot assign a private weight to one corner unless the depth and the receptive field grow enough to reach it. Representation learning, as the next chapter defines it, looks for a short vector computed by shared weights.

The same count explains patches. A cube of side $256$ holds $16777216$ voxels. One patient-level label supervises that whole cube if you train only the final class head. Self-supervision in [ch. 6](#ch6) builds losses on the voxels themselves so that the shared kernels see more than one bit of supervision per scan.

### 0.4 Sample covariance

Let the rows of the data matrix be centred. With $n$ rows, the sample covariance divides the Gram matrix by $n - 1$.
$$
C = \frac{1}{n-1} X^\top X.
$$
The matrix $C$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are non-negative. Exercise 2 uses 40 points in dimension 2 and prints the largest eigenvalue.

That eigenvalue is the largest variance of a unit-length linear image of the sample. [ch. 1](#ch1) proves the variational claim. You do not need the proof to read the printed number. You do need the divisor: replacing $39$ by $40$ changes the value.

::: key
[Key — chapter 0]{.tag} A descent step on the logistic loss moves the logit by the gap between the label and the predicted probability.
$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z} = q - y.
$$
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The empirical risk is the average loss on the $n$ training pairs. It is not the risk on a new hospital.
-   For a binary logistic loss, the derivative in the logit equals the predicted probability minus the label.
-   At logit $1$ and label $1$, the probability is $0.7311$, the loss is $0.3133$, and the derivative is $-0.2689$.
-   A $3 \times 3$ convolution with eight filters has $80$ parameters. A dense weight per pixel of a $256 \times 256$ image has $65536$ parameters for one output.
:::

## 1. Representations, principal components and latent factors {#ch1}

A representation is the vector you hand to a simple predictor. Hand-built features were edges, textures and atlas coordinates. This chapter defines the map, proves which linear map maximises variance, and shows why an isotropic Gaussian latent code does not name its own axes. Those two results are the linear and the generative halves of the official topic "representation learning", including disentangled generative models.

Bengio, Courville and Vincent (2013) describe the goal as a map that is discriminative and organised. Discriminative means a simple function of the vector predicts the label. Organised means a coordinate, or a direction, tracks a factor a person can name: a position, a scanner, a pathology. The course never assumes that training produces such axes by itself. Proposition 1.4 is the obstruction.

### 1.1 The map

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Representation]{.tag} A representation is a map $\varphi$ from the image space to a vector space $Z$. A linear probe is a predictor that reads $\varphi(x)$ and does not change $\varphi$. Fine-tuning changes $\varphi$ as well. Both names return in [ch. 2](#ch2).

The dimension of $Z$ is the length of the vector. For a radiograph, the raw dimension is the number of pixels. A representation of length $32$ or $512$ is the object the later losses train.
:::

An autoencoder pairs $\varphi$ with a decoder $g$. The reconstruction loss is the mean squared error between $x$ and $g(\varphi(x))$. If both maps are linear and the loss is squared error, a global minimum reconstructs through a principal subspace (Baldi and Hornik, 1989). The axes inside that subspace are not unique. The next proposition fixes one variational choice of axis. It does not claim that every autoencoder returns that axis.

### 1.2 The leading principal component

Let $\Sigma$ be a $d \times d$ covariance, hence symmetric and positive semidefinite. A unit vector $u$ defines a one-dimensional projection. The variance of that projection is the scalar $u^\top \Sigma u$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Rayleigh quotient]{.tag} The maximum of $u^\top \Sigma u$ over unit vectors $u$ equals the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$. A unit eigenvector for $\lambda_{\max}$ attains it.

::: proof
The spectral theorem writes $\Sigma = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ with $\Lambda$ diagonal and $Q$ orthogonal. Set $v = Q^\top u$. Then $v$ is a unit vector, because $Q$ preserves Euclidean length.

The quadratic form becomes $\sum_i \lambda_i v_i^2$. Every $\lambda_i$ is at most $\lambda_{\max}$, and $\sum_i v_i^2 = 1$, so the sum is at most $\lambda_{\max}$.

Equality holds when $v$ is supported on the largest eigenvalue, which means $u$ is a matching unit eigenvector. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Pearson (1901) studied the closest-fit line. The proposition is the variance form of that line. The fraction of variance kept by the leading axis is $\lambda_{\max}$ divided by the trace of $\Sigma$. The trace equals the sum of the coordinate variances.

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — A diagonal covariance]{.tag} Let $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$. The eigenvalues are $4$ and $1$. The maximum variance is $4$, at the first canonical vector. The trace is $5$, so the leading axis keeps the fraction $4/5 = 0.8$.

The point $(2, 3)$ projects to $(2, 0)$. The residual is $(0, 3)$, and the squared error is $9$. Projecting on the second axis instead keeps variance $1$ and is worse for the Rayleigh quotient. A cloud with $\Sigma$ equal to a multiple of the identity has no preferred axis. That cloud is the finite-sample cousin of the rotation in Proposition 1.4.
:::

### 1.3 Latent factors and a rotation

A generative model draws a latent code $z$ and then an image from a decoder. Disentanglement asks the coordinates of $z$ to match separate factors. The standard normal prior does not, by itself, mark which coordinate is which.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Rotation ambiguity]{.tag} Let $z$ have law $N(0, I_k)$. Let $R$ be an orthogonal matrix of the same size. Then $Rz$ has the same law as $z$.

For any decoder $f$, the image $f(z)$ equals the image obtained after rotating the code and undoing that rotation inside the decoder. The law of the image does not determine the coordinates of $z$.

::: proof
The covariance of $Rz$ is $R I_k R^\top = I_k$, and the mean stays $0$. A Gaussian is determined by its mean and covariance, so $Rz$ has law $N(0, I_k)$.

Set $u = Rz$. Then $f(z) = f(R^\top u)$. As $z$ runs through its law, $u$ runs through the same law, and the pushforward images coincide.

The coordinates of $u$ are mixtures of the coordinates of $z$ whenever $R$ is not a signed permutation. The marginal law of the image is unchanged by that mixture. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Beta-VAE penalty]{.tag} The beta-VAE objective of Higgins and coauthors (2017) is a reconstruction term plus a positive multiple $\beta$ of the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the encoder's conditional law of $z$ to the standard normal. The case $\beta = 1$ is the variational autoencoder of Kingma and Welling (2014).
$$
L_\beta(x) = L_{\mathrm{rec}}(x) + \beta \, \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\big).
$$

The prior density of $N(0, I_k)$ is constant on spheres. It does not prefer an orientation. Raising $\beta$ presses the code toward that prior. It does not, by the proposition, choose axes. [ch. 8](#ch8) points to the empirical study of Locatello and coauthors (2019).
:::

A diagonal Gaussian encoder is an extra constraint. The course does not claim that the diagonal removes the ambiguity. It claims only what Proposition 1.4 proves: the law of the images is not enough.

::: key
[Key — chapter 1]{.tag} Among unit directions, the variance of a linear projection is the Rayleigh quotient, and its maximum is the largest eigenvalue.
$$
\max_{\|u\|=1} u^\top \Sigma u = \lambda_{\max}.
$$
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   A representation is a map from the image to a vector. A probe reads the vector. Fine-tuning changes the map.
-   The leading principal component maximises variance among unit directions. On $\mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$ it keeps the fraction $0.8$.
-   A linear autoencoder can recover the principal subspace and still fail to name unique axes inside it.
-   If the latent prior is isotropic Gaussian, an orthogonal change of coordinates leaves the law of the images unchanged.
:::

## 2. Transfer learning {#ch2}

Transfer learning reuses a representation trained on a source task. The target task in this course is often a small labelled medical set. The source is a large set of natural images, or another medical collection. This chapter defines the two ways to reuse the map and proves that a probe has a convex training problem. The practical question is the number of free weights compared with the number of labels.

Yosinski, Clune, Bengio and Lipson (2014) observed, on natural images, that early-layer features transfer more readily than the features in the last layer. Pan and Yang (2010) survey the vocabulary. Esteva and coauthors (2017) fine-tuned an ImageNet-pretrained network on clinical skin images. Raghu, Zhang, Kleinberg and Bengio (2019) compare ImageNet initialisation with training from scratch on medical tasks and find that the gain is largest when the labelled medical set is small. The proposition below is the convexity reason a small set still has a well-posed probe.

### 2.1 Probe and fine-tuning

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Frozen probe and fine-tuning]{.tag} Fix a representation $\varphi$. A frozen probe chooses a matrix $W$ and a bias, and predicts from the logit vector $W \varphi(x) + b$. The map $\varphi$ stays at its source value.

Fine-tuning lets the parameters inside $\varphi$ move, usually from that same source value. The probe is a convex problem under Proposition 2.2. Fine-tuning is not, once $\varphi$ contains a nonlinearity.
:::

The source value may be the result of supervised training or of the self-supervised training in [ch. 6](#ch6). Transfer does not require the source labels to share a meaning with the target labels. It requires the vector $\varphi(x)$ to make the target easier. If the vector mostly encodes a scanner, transfer carries the scanner. That failure is the subject of [ch. 3](#ch3).

### 2.2 Convexity

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — The probe is convex]{.tag} Fix $\varphi$. For binary labels, the mean logistic loss of a probe is a convex function of the probe weights.

::: proof
By the computation in Proposition 0.2, the scalar loss is convex in the logit. Its second derivative in the logit equals $q(1-q)$, which is at least $0$.

The logit of a probe is an affine function of the weights: a dot product with the frozen vector $\varphi(x)$, plus a bias. An affine precomposition preserves convexity.

The mean of convex functions is convex. A local minimum of the probe loss is therefore a global minimum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same argument applies to the multi-class cross-entropy, because that loss is convex in the vector of logits and the logits are affine in $W$. The course uses the binary proof, which is complete, as the model. Fine-tuning breaks the argument at the first step that is false: the map from the inner weights to the logit is no longer affine.

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — Forty labels and a vector of length 512]{.tag} Suppose $\varphi(x)$ lies in $\mathbb{R}^{512}$ and the target has two classes. A probe has $512 \times 2$ matrix entries and $2$ biases, hence $1026$ parameters. The training set in this example has $40$ labelled images.

Forty images cannot determine $1026$ weights without a preference for small weights, but the objective stays convex, so gradient descent does not stop at a bad local minimum of the probe. A network with $10^{6}$ trainable weights on the same $40$ images has far more free parameters than labels, and the objective is not convex. Raghu and coauthors (2019) is the empirical companion: look first at whether the labelled set is small before you pay for full fine-tuning.

Ex. 4 counts a smaller encoder, from length $784$ to length $32$ and then to $10$ classes, and gets $25450$ parameters. The hidden vector of length $32$ is the representation. The last layer is a probe on it.
:::

On a medical set, "small" is a comparison of labelled patients with free weights, not a universal cutoff. The course states no official cutoff. The worked comparison is $40$ images against $1026$ probe weights and against $10^{6}$ fine-tuned weights.

::: key
[Key — chapter 2]{.tag} With the representation held fixed, the mean logistic loss of a linear probe is a convex function of the probe weights.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   A frozen probe trains a linear classifier on a fixed vector. Fine-tuning also moves the map that builds the vector.
-   The probe loss is convex in its weights because the logit is affine and the logistic loss is convex in the logit.
-   A two-class probe on a vector of length $512$ has $1026$ parameters. Forty labels do not determine a network with $10^{6}$ weights.
-   Published comparisons find the largest gain from ImageNet initialisation when the labelled medical set is small.
:::

## 3. Domain adaptation {#ch3}

A representation trained on one distribution can fail on another even when the label set has the same names. Zech and coauthors (2018) document that failure for pneumonia classifiers across hospitals. This chapter writes the failure as a change of distribution, proves the identity that reweights a source sample when only the covariates shift, and defines the H-divergence that a domain classifier estimates.

The official topic is domain adaptation. The method named at the end, domain-adversarial training (Ganin and coauthors, 2016), trains the representation to make the divergence small. The proved statement is the weight identity. The adversarial method is the algorithm you implement when the identity's hypothesis fails.

### 3.1 Covariate shift

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Covariate shift]{.tag} Write $p_S$ and $p_T$ for the source and target distributions of the pair $(X, Y)$. Covariate shift means
$$
p_S(y \mid x) = p_T(y \mid x)
$$
whenever both sides are defined, while $p_S(x)$ and $p_T(x)$ may differ.

Label shift is the symmetric case: the class-conditional laws of $x$ agree, and the class frequencies differ. A scanner that changes how a disease looks in the image breaks covariate shift, because the conditional of $Y$ given $X$ has changed.
:::

Under covariate shift, a loss computed on source pairs is the wrong expectation for the target, but each source pair can be reweighted. The weight is the ratio of the two densities of $X$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Importance weights]{.tag} Assume covariate shift, and assume $p_T(x) = 0$ whenever $p_S(x) = 0$. For any predictor $h$ and any non-negative loss,
$$
R_T(h) = \mathbb{E}_S\left[ \frac{p_T(X)}{p_S(X)} \, \ell(h(X), Y) \right].
$$

::: proof
Start from the target expectation of the loss. Factor the target joint density as $p_T(y \mid x) \, p_T(x)$.

Replace $p_T(y \mid x)$ by $p_S(y \mid x)$. Multiply and divide by $p_S(x)$. The hypothesis on the supports keeps the ratio finite.

The integral is now the source expectation of the weighted loss. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The identity says the target risk is a weighted source risk. It does not say the weights are easy to estimate. A ratio of densities in a high-dimensional image space is a hard estimation problem. That is why adaptation often matches distributions in the representation space rather than in the pixel space.

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — A one-dimensional weight]{.tag} Let the source law of $X$ be standard normal and the target law be normal with mean $0.5$ and variance $1$. At $x = 1$ the log weight equals $-0.5(1-0.5)^2 + 0.5(1)^2 = 0.375$. The weight is $e^{0.375} = 1.455$ to three decimals.

A source point at $x = 1$ counts $1.455$ times more in the target risk than in the source risk. Points on the far left are down-weighted. Ex. 6 draws a three-dimensional version of a mean shift and prints the norm of the difference of sample means.

If a balanced domain classifier has error $0.2$, then $|1 - 2 \times 0.2| = 0.6$. Under Definition 3.4 that gap of $0.6$ witnesses a divergence of at least $1.2$.
:::

### 3.2 The H-divergence

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — H-divergence]{.tag} For a class $\mathcal{H}$ of classifiers with values in $\{0, 1\}$,
$$
d_{\mathcal{H}}(D_S, D_T) = 2 \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \big| \Pr_S(h = 1) - \Pr_T(h = 1) \big|.
$$

The divergence lies in the interval from $0$ to $2$. It is $0$ when no classifier in the class can tell the two distributions apart.
:::

Train a domain classifier on a balanced mixture, with source labelled $1$ and target labelled $0$. Its error $\varepsilon$ satisfies $1 - 2\varepsilon = \Pr_S(h=1) - \Pr_T(h=1)$. The absolute value is the gap inside the supremum. Twice that gap is the contribution of this one classifier to the divergence. If the classifier attains the supremum, the divergence equals that contribution.

Ben-David, Blitzer, Crammer, Kulesza, Pereira and Vaughan (2010) use this divergence to bound the target risk by the source risk, the divergence, and the joint error of the best hypothesis. The course does not reprove that uniform-convergence bound. It uses the definition, which you can estimate with a classifier, and the weight identity, which is proved.

Ganin and coauthors (2016) attach a domain classifier to the representation and reverse the gradient of the domain loss in the encoder. The encoder keeps the label loss small and pushes the divergence down. Tzeng, Hoffman, Saenko and Darrell (2017) train a separate adversarial objective with the same aim. Use those algorithms when covariate shift is false. A new scanner often makes it false.

::: note
[When the weight identity does not apply]{.tag} If the scanner changes $p(y \mid x)$, reweighting $p(x)$ leaves a biased target risk. A corner token that predicts the hospital is a feature you want the divergence term to erase, not a covariate you want to reweight into the test set.
:::

::: key
[Key — chapter 3]{.tag} Under covariate shift, the target risk equals a source expectation with weight $p_T(x)/p_S(x)$.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Covariate shift keeps $p(y \mid x)$ and lets $p(x)$ change. A scanner that changes the look of the disease breaks that hypothesis.
-   When the hypothesis holds, each source loss is multiplied by the density ratio of the covariates.
-   At $x = 1$, a shift of the mean from $0$ to $0.5$ gives the weight $1.455$.
-   A domain error of $0.2$ on a balanced mixture witnesses an H-divergence of at least $1.2$ under Definition 3.4.
:::

## 4. Multi-task learning {#ch4}

Multi-task learning trains one representation for several predictions. A medical network may segment an organ and regress its volume from the same encoder. Caruana (1997) argued that the extra tasks act as a preference on the shared map: a direction that helps only one task and hurts the others is a poor shared feature. This chapter writes the joint loss, proves it stays convex when each task is convex and the weights are non-negative, and computes a case where the task gradients disagree.

### 4.1 The joint objective

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Shared encoder]{.tag} Let $\varphi_\theta$ be an encoder with parameters $\theta$. Task $t$ has a head $h_t$ and a loss $L_t(\theta)$. Non-negative weights $w_t$ define
$$
L(\theta) = \sum_t w_t L_t(\theta).
$$

The heads may have private parameters. The shared object is $\theta$. If a weight is zero, that task does not affect $\theta$.
:::

Kendall, Gal and Cipolla (2018) replace hand-chosen weights, in a regression setting, by a penalty that depends on a positive scale $\sigma_t$ for each task. For squared losses their objective has the form
$$
\sum_t \left( \frac{1}{2\sigma_t^2} L_t + \log \sigma_t \right).
$$

A task with a large estimated noise $\sigma_t$ receives a small coefficient in front of $L_t$. The $\log \sigma_t$ term stops the scale from drifting to infinity. The course uses this formula as their weighting, not as a theorem proved here. The convexity proposition uses fixed weights.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Non-negative weights preserve convexity]{.tag} If every $L_t$ is convex and every $w_t$ is non-negative, then $L$ is convex.

::: proof
Fix two parameter vectors and a scalar $\alpha$ in the unit interval. Convexity of $L_t$ gives $L_t$ at the mixture bounded by the mixture of the values.

Multiply by $w_t$. The inequality direction is unchanged because $w_t$ is non-negative. Sum over tasks.

The left side is $L$ at the mixture. The right side is the mixture of the values of $L$. That is convexity of $L$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The encoder of a deep network is not a convex function of $\theta$. The proposition applies to the heads when the encoder is frozen, and to any task loss that is already convex in the shared parameters. It tells you that the obstruction in the next example is the sign of the gradients, not a failure of the algebra of the weights.

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Opposite gradients]{.tag} Let the shared parameter be a scalar. The derivative of task 1 is 4 and the derivative of task 2 is $-1$. With equal weights the joint derivative is 3. A small descent step decreases the parameter, which decreases task 1 and increases task 2.

With weights 1 and 4 the joint derivative is $1 \times 4 + 4 \times (-1) = 0$. The weighted objective is stationary, and neither loss is forced down.

No step decreases both losses at this point. A decrease of $L_1$ needs a negative step, because the derivative is positive. A decrease of $L_2$ needs a positive step, because its derivative is negative. The two demands contradict. Ex. 7 asks you to write this argument.

For the Kendall weighting, take task losses 0.4 and 1.2 with scales 1 and 2. The objective equals $0.2 + 0.15 + \log 2$, which is 1.043 to three decimals.

The noisier task is down-weighted from 1.2 to 0.15 inside that sum, before the $\log 2$ penalty.
:::

In a segmentation-plus-volume model, a step that improves the volume and erodes the mask is the situation in the example. The remedy the definition allows is a different pair $(w_1, w_2)$, or a stop on the shared encoder while one head finishes. The course does not claim a universal best weight.

::: key
[Key — chapter 4]{.tag} The gradient of a weighted sum of task losses is the same weighted sum of the task gradients. Opposite signs cannot be removed by positive weights.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   One encoder can feed several heads. The joint loss is a non-negative combination of the task losses.
-   Non-negative weights preserve convexity. They do not preserve a descent direction for every task.
-   Derivatives $4$ and $-1$ give a joint derivative $3$ at equal weights, and $0$ at weights $1$ and $4$.
-   With scales $1$ and $2$ and losses $0.4$ and $1.2$, the Kendall objective equals $1.043$.
:::

## 5. Knowledge distillation {#ch5}

Knowledge distillation trains a small network, the student, to match a large network, the teacher. Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015) replace hard labels by soft targets, the teacher's class probabilities at a temperature $T$. A hospital may run the teacher once, offline, and ship the student. This chapter defines the soft targets, proves the entropy bound that says how uncertain a probability vector can be, and computes the same logits at two temperatures.

Uncertainty enters here as the entropy of the predictive distribution. A vector near the uniform distribution has high entropy and does not commit to a class. Calibration, ensembles and dropout estimators are left to [ch. 8](#ch8). The bound proved now is what makes the temperature meaningful.

### 5.1 Soft targets

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Temperature softmax]{.tag} For logits $z_1, \ldots, z_K$ and a temperature $T > 0$,
$$
q_i(T) = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp(z_j / T)}.
$$

The soft target is the teacher's probability vector at that temperature. The student uses the same temperature while it matches the vector. At test time the temperature returns to 1. As the temperature grows, each logit divided by the temperature tends to 0, so the vector tends to the uniform vector.
:::

Hinton, Vinyals and Dean multiply the soft-target loss by $T^2$ when they form the training gradient. The factor keeps the scale of the gradient from collapsing as $T$ grows. The course records their factor as part of the method. The proved statement is the entropy bound, which does not depend on that factor.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Entropy bound]{.tag} Let $q$ be a probability vector on $K$ classes, and let $H(q) = -\sum_i q_i \log q_i$. Then $H(q) \le \log K$, with equality at the uniform vector.

::: proof
Let $u$ be the uniform vector, with every coordinate equal to $1/K$. The Kullback-Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, u)$ is non-negative.

Expand the divergence. It equals $-H(q) + \log K$, because $-\log u_i = \log K$ and the $q_i$ sum to $1$.

Non-negativity rearranges into $H(q) \le \log K$. Equality holds when $q = u$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The logarithm is natural in the proof and in the numerical values below. A change of base multiplies both sides by the same constant. For $K = 3$, the bound is $\log 3 = 1.099$ to three decimals. A soft target that reaches an entropy above that number is wrongly computed.

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — Two temperatures]{.tag} Take logits 2, 0 and $-1$. At temperature 1 the probabilities are 0.844, 0.114 and 0.042 to three decimals. The entropy is 0.524.

At temperature 4 the probabilities are 0.481, 0.292 and 0.227. The entropy is 1.048. The mass has moved toward the uniform vector, and the entropy has moved toward 1.099, in agreement with Definition 5.1 and Proposition 5.2.

A student with logits 1.5, 0.2 and $-0.5$, also read at temperature 4, has probabilities 0.429, 0.310 and 0.260. The Kullback-Leibler divergence from the teacher to this student is 0.0058 to four decimals. Exercise 8 asks for the two teacher vectors and the two entropies.
:::

The hard label is a one-hot vector. Its entropy is $0$. Matching only the hard label throws away the teacher's ranking of the wrong classes. The soft target keeps that ranking. Distillation is useful when the student has fewer parameters than the teacher and you still want the ranking. The project in the assessment section fixes a synthetic image task where that comparison is measurable.

::: key
[Key — chapter 5]{.tag} Raising the temperature flattens the softmax toward the uniform vector, and no probability vector has entropy above $\log K$.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Soft targets are the teacher's softmax probabilities at a temperature $T$. Test-time prediction uses $T = 1$.
-   The entropy of a probability vector on $K$ classes is at most $\log K$.
-   Logits 2, 0 and $-1$ give entropy 0.524 at temperature 1 and entropy 1.048 at temperature 4.
-   The factor $T^2$ in front of the soft loss is the scaling stated by Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015).
:::

## 6. Self-supervised learning and foundation models {#ch6}

Self-supervised learning builds a representation without class labels. A pretext task defines the loss from the image alone. A foundation model, in the sense used here, is a network pretrained on a large collection and then adapted to several downstream tasks with few labels. This chapter proves a one-line form of the contrastive loss and places rotation prediction, contrastive pairs and masked patches on one ladder.

Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi and Hinton (2020) train on two random views of one image and treat the other images in the batch as negatives (SimCLR). He, Fan, Wu, Xie and Girshick (2020) keep a memory of negatives (MoCo). He, Chen, Xie, Li, Dollár and Girshick (2022) mask patches and reconstruct them (MAE). van den Oord, Li and Vinyals (2018) introduced the InfoNCE loss that SimCLR uses. Gidaris, Singh and Komodakis (2018) use a simpler pretext: predict which of the four rotations was applied.

### 6.1 The contrastive loss

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — One-negative InfoNCE]{.tag} Let $s^+$ be the similarity of an anchor with a positive view, and let $s^-$ be the similarity with one negative. For a temperature $\tau > 0$,
$$
\ell = - \log \frac{\exp(s^+ / \tau)}{\exp(s^+ / \tau) + \exp(s^- / \tau)}.
$$

A full batch replaces the single negative by a sum. The one-negative case is the one proved below. Similarity in SimCLR is a dot product of normalised vectors.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Softplus form]{.tag} The one-negative loss equals
$$
\ell = \log \big(1 + \exp((s^- - s^+) / \tau)\big).
$$

::: proof
Divide the numerator and the denominator of Definition 6.1 by $\exp(s^+ / \tau)$.

The fraction becomes $1 / (1 + \exp((s^- - s^+)/\tau))$. The loss is the negative log of that fraction.

Negative log of a reciprocal is the log of the denominator. That denominator is the expression in the statement. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The loss is the softplus of the margin $(s^- - s^+)/\tau$. It is always positive. It is small when the positive similarity exceeds the negative one by several times $\tau$. The gradient in $s^+$ is negative, so descent increases $s^+$. The gradient in $s^-$ is positive, so descent decreases $s^-$.

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — A margin of 1]{.tag} Take $s^+ = 1$, $s^- = 0$ and $\tau = 0.5$. The margin over temperature is $(0 - 1)/0.5 = -2$. The loss equals $\log(1 + e^{-2}) = 0.1269$ to four decimals.

If the negative had been identical to the positive, the margin would be $0$ and the loss would be $\log 2 = 0.6931$. The gap between $0.1269$ and $0.6931$ is the reward for separating the negative. Ex. 9 asks what happens when the "negative" is a second crop of the same tumour.
:::

### 6.2 From a pretext task to a foundation model

Rotation prediction is a four-way classification. You rotate the image by $0$, $90$, $180$ or $270$ degrees and ask the network to name the angle. The loss is an ordinary cross-entropy. The representation is the vector before the four-way head. The method needs no second view and no large batch. It is a baseline, not the strongest pretext in the papers above.

Contrastive pretraining needs an agreement about what a positive pair is. Two crops of one photograph are a standard positive pair. Two crops of one tumour are a dangerous negative if the batch happens to treat them as distinct images. The softplus then pushes those two tumour vectors apart. A later linear probe must map both vectors to the same label. Ex. 9 develops that failure.

Masked autoencoders hide a fraction of the patches and train the network to reconstruct the missing intensities. The loss is a reconstruction error on the hidden sites, in the spirit of the autoencoder of [ch. 1](#ch1), with a transformer encoder as in [ch. 7](#ch7). The representation is the encoder's output, not the reconstructed pixels.

A cube of side $256$ has $16777216$ voxels and often one patient-level label. The pretext loss supervises the encoder from the voxels. The downstream probe supervises it from the label, sometimes from a few dozen labels, which is the regime of Proposition 2.2. Calling the pretrained encoder a foundation model records the reuse across tasks. It does not record a guarantee that the medical probe will beat a probe trained from scratch. That comparison is an experiment, and it is one of the projects.

::: key
[Key — chapter 6]{.tag} With one negative, the contrastive loss is the softplus of $(s^- - s^+)/\tau$. Descent increases the positive similarity and decreases the negative one.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   A pretext task defines a loss from the image alone. Rotation prediction is a four-way cross-entropy.
-   With one negative, InfoNCE equals $\log(1 + \exp((s^- - s^+)/\tau))$.
-   Similarities $1$ and $0$ at temperature $0.5$ give the loss $0.1269$.
-   A foundation model is a pretrained encoder reused on later tasks. A $256^3$ volume has $16777216$ voxels and may have a single label.
:::

## 7. Attention, transformers and explanations {#ch7}

Attention builds a new vector for each token as a weighted sum of value vectors. Transformers stack that operation with a shared map applied at every token (Vaswani and coauthors, 2017). Dosovitskiy and coauthors (2021) cut an image into patches and run a transformer on the patches. This chapter proves that the weights form a convex combination, computes a two-token example, and separates that weight from a gradient-based localisation map.

Interpretability, in the sense of the official list, is the question of which input region the prediction used. Uncertainty, already bounded in [ch. 5](#ch5), is the entropy of the class distribution. Neither question is answered by reading a single attention weight. The zero-value calculation shows why.

### 7.1 Scaled dot-product attention

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Attention]{.tag} Let $q$ be a query vector and let $(k_i, v_i)$ be key-value pairs, with keys of the same dimension $d$ as the query. The weights and the output are
$$
w_i = \frac{\exp(q \cdot k_i / \sqrt{d})}{\sum_j \exp(q \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d})}, \qquad o = \sum_i w_i v_i.
$$

The scale $\sqrt{d}$ keeps the dot products from growing with the dimension. The values may have a different dimension from the keys.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Convex combination]{.tag} The weights are non-negative and sum to $1$. The output is a convex combination of the value vectors. If a value vector is $0$, that token does not change the output.

::: proof
Each exponential is positive, and the weights divide by their sum, so each $w_i$ is positive and the sum of the $w_i$ is $1$. A weighted sum with those two properties is a convex combination.

If $v_i = 0$, the term $w_i v_i$ is the zero vector. Dropping it does not change $o$. The weight $w_i$ can stay large. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 7.3 — Two tokens]{.tag} Take dimension 1, query 1, keys 1 and 0, and values 2 and 5. The scores are 1 and 0. The weights are $e/(1+e) = 0.7311$ and $1/(1+e) = 0.2689$ to four decimals.

The output is $0.7311 \times 2 + 0.2689 \times 5 = 2.8068$. Set the first value to $0$ and the second value to $2e + 5 = 10.4366$. The weights are unchanged, because they do not depend on the values. The output is unchanged, because $0.2689 \times 10.4366 = 2.8068$. The first token still holds weight $0.7311$ and contributes nothing. Ex. 10 asks for this construction.
:::

A vision transformer cuts an image into patches of size $16 \times 16$. On a $224 \times 224$ image there are $14 \times 14 = 196$ patches. A class token brings the sequence length to $197$. Each patch is flattened and multiplied by a matrix. A learned vector is added to mark position. A block adds the attention output back to the tokens and applies the same two-layer map at each token, with a residual link around each of those two steps (Dosovitskiy and coauthors, 2021).

### 7.2 Localisation and entropy

::: def
[Definition 7.4 — Grad-CAM weight]{.tag} Let $A$ be one feature map and let $y$ be the score of a class before the softmax. The Grad-CAM weight of Selvaraju and coauthors (2017) is the average, over the spatial sites, of $\partial y / \partial A$. The localisation map is the positive part of the weighted sum of the maps.

On a map with two sites, values 1 and 4, and gradients 0 and 2, the average gradient is 1. The localisation map equals the feature map itself, the pair (1, 4). The second site is brighter because it was brighter in the feature map, and the weight happened to be positive.
:::

The average gradient can be negative. The positive part then erases that map. A large attention weight is not this gradient. Proposition 7.2 shows a large weight on a zero value. [ch. 8](#ch8) cites the sanity checks that ask whether a localisation map changes when the network is randomised.

Predictive uncertainty for a single softmax is the entropy $H(q)$ from Proposition 5.2. Monte Carlo dropout (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016) draws $T$ random masks at test time, averages the probability vectors, and reads the entropy of the average. The average is
$$
\bar q = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} q^{(t)}.
$$

The entropy of $\bar q$ is at most $\log K$ by the same proposition. A value near the bound means the averaged predictor does not commit. Deep ensembles average networks trained from different initialisations (Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel and Blundell, 2017). Both estimators are used in [ch. 8](#ch8). The formula to compute by hand in this chapter remains the two-token attention output.

::: key
[Key — chapter 7]{.tag} Attention outputs a convex combination of the values. A token with value zero does not move the output, whatever its weight.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Scaled dot-product attention builds non-negative weights that sum to $1$, then sums the values with those weights.
-   Keys 1 and 0 with query 1 give weights 0.7311 and 0.2689, and values 2 and 5 give the output 2.8068.
-   Replacing the values by $0$ and $10.4366$ keeps both the weights and the output. The large weight explains nothing by itself.
-   A Grad-CAM weight is an average gradient of the class score. Predictive entropy is the uncertainty of a probability vector.
:::

## 8. Research directions and open problems {#ch8}

The eight lectures proved the identities you can check by hand. This chapter lists three research questions that those identities do not close, and a reading order for about four hours. The voice is the literature's. Nothing here is a result of these notes.

### 8.1 Disentangled factors

Proposition 1.4 shows that an isotropic Gaussian prior does not mark axes. Higgins and coauthors (2017) increase the weight $\beta$ on the divergence to the standard normal and report latent coordinates that track simple visual factors on synthetic scenes. Locatello, Bauer, Lucic, Gelly, Schölkopf, Bachem and coauthors (2019) argue that unsupervised disentanglement is not identified without an inductive bias on the model class, and that random seeds and hyperparameters can dominate the comparison of methods.

The open question for medical images is narrower. A factor you can name, such as scanner vendor against lesion size, is useful only if it stays stable when the decoder class changes. The rotation proof says the law of the images will not force that stability. An inductive bias might. Which bias is enough for radiographs is not settled by the proposition.

### 8.2 Uncertainty

Proposition 5.2 bounds the entropy of one softmax. Gal and Ghahramani (2016) read a trained dropout network as a variational approximation and average several stochastic passes. Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel and Blundell (2017) average an ensemble instead. Guo, Pleiss, Sun and Weinberger (2017) show that modern networks can be accurate and still poorly calibrated: the predicted probability is not the frequency of correctness.

The open question is whether a student distilled in [ch. 5](#ch5) can match the teacher's entropy, not only its argmax. Soft targets carry some of that information. A quantitative guarantee, under a stated distance between student and teacher, is not the entropy bound.

### 8.3 Explanations that survive a check

Definition 7.4 gives a Grad-CAM weight, and Proposition 7.2 shows an attention weight that does not change the output. Selvaraju and coauthors (2017) define the localisation map used in many medical papers. Adebayo, Gilmer, Muelly, Goodfellow, Hardt and Kim (2018) propose a sanity check: randomise the model in a cascade and ask whether the map changes. A map that stays still when the weights change is not an explanation of those weights. Jain and Wallace (2019) argue that attention weights remain a weak explanation even when they correlate with other measures.

The open question is which map, on a chest radiograph, changes under their randomisation and still highlights the lesion rather than the corner token of Zech and coauthors (2018). A passing sanity check is not a clinical validation. It is a filter that removes maps independent of the model.

### 8.4 A four-hour reading order

-   First hour. Reread Proposition 1.4. Read the objective in Higgins and coauthors (2017) and write the role of $\beta$ in one paragraph of your own.
-   Second hour. Read the claim of Locatello and coauthors (2019) that unsupervised comparisons need a bias. List one bias you would impose on a radiograph model, and one failure if the bias is wrong.
-   Third hour. Compare one stochastic pass of Gal and Ghahramani (2016) with the ensemble average of Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel and Blundell (2017). State which average you can run on a laptop.
-   Fourth hour. Apply the randomisation question of Adebayo and coauthors (2018) to the two-site map in Definition 7.4. Say what a map that ignores the gradient would look like on that example.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 8

-   An isotropic prior plus a flexible decoder does not identify latent axes. Extra bias may, and may also be wrong.
-   Entropy bounds one softmax. Calibration and ensembles ask whether the number is a frequency.
-   A localisation map that does not change when the network is randomised is not an explanation of that network.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Logistic loss at logit 1.** Let the logit be $z = 1$ and the label be $y = 1$. Compute the sigmoid probability, the binary cross-entropy, and the derivative of the loss with respect to $z$.

    *Solution*: Proposition 0.2. The probability is $0.7311$. The loss is $0.3133$. The derivative is $-0.2689$, to four decimals. The derivative is negative, so a descent step increases the logit.

2.  **★ Top variance of a seeded sample.** The fence draws $40$ centred points in dimension $2$ and prints the largest eigenvalue of the sample covariance with divisor $39$. Run it and say what the number is.

```python
import numpy
rng = numpy.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(40, 2))
X = X - X.mean(axis=0)
C = (X.T @ X) / 39
evals = numpy.linalg.eigvalsh(C)
print(round(float(evals[-1]), 4))
```

    *Solution*: The fence prints $1.1154$. That number is the largest eigenvalue of this seeded covariance. It is the quantity Definition 0.4 asks you to read. Chapter 1 proves it is the maximum variance of a unit linear projection.

3.  **★ Projection onto the leading axis.** Let the covariance be $\mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$. Take the unit vector $(1, 0)$. Give the variance of the projection, the fraction of the total variance, and the squared error when $(2, 3)$ is reconstructed from that projection.

    *Solution*: Example 1.3. The variance is $4$. The trace is $5$, so the fraction is $0.8$. The reconstruction is $(2, 0)$ and the squared error is $9$.

4.  **★ Parameter count of a small encoder.** A layer maps length $784$ to length $32$ with a bias. A second layer maps length $32$ to length $10$ with a bias. How many parameters are there, and which vector is the representation?

    *Solution*: The first layer has $784 \times 32 + 32 = 25120$ parameters. The second has $32 \times 10 + 10 = 330$ parameters. The total is $25450$. The hidden vector of length $32$ is the representation. The second layer is a probe.

5.  **★★ Convexity of a linear probe.** The feature is the scalar $1$ and the label is $1$. The loss is the binary cross-entropy of the sigmoid of a weight $w$. Compute the loss at $w = 0$, at $w = 2$ and at $w = 1$. Check the chord inequality. Then prove convexity in the weights for a frozen feature of any length.

    *Solution*: The losses are $0.6931$, $0.1269$ and $0.3133$. The chord average is $0.4100$, which lies above $0.3133$. Proposition 2.2: the second derivative in the logit is $q(1-q) \ge 0$, and the logit is affine in the weights.

6.  **★★ Mean shift between two seeded samples.** The fence draws $200$ source points from the standard normal in dimension $3$ and $200$ target points from the normal with mean $0.8$ in every coordinate. It prints the Euclidean norm of the difference of the sample means. Also compute $|1 - 2\varepsilon|$ and the witnessed H-divergence when a balanced domain classifier has error $\varepsilon = 0.2$.

```python
import numpy
rng = numpy.random.default_rng(0)
src = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=(200, 3))
tgt = rng.normal(loc=0.8, scale=1.0, size=(200, 3))
delta = tgt.mean(axis=0) - src.mean(axis=0)
print(round(float(numpy.linalg.norm(delta)), 4))
```

    *Solution*: The fence prints $1.3727$. The population shift $(0.8, 0.8, 0.8)$ has norm $0.8 \sqrt{3} = 1.3856$, so the sample is close to that shift. For the classifier, $|1 - 2 \times 0.2| = 0.6$, and Definition 3.4 witnesses a divergence of at least $1.2$.

7.  **★★ Task gradients with opposite signs.** The shared parameter is a scalar. The derivative of task 1 is $4$ and the derivative of task 2 is $-1$. Compute the joint derivative at equal weights and at weights $1$ and $4$. Show that no single step decreases both losses.

    *Solution*: Example 4.3. Equal weights give derivative $3$. Weights $1$ and $4$ give derivative $0$. A step that decreases task 1 is negative. A step that decreases task 2 is positive. No real step is both.

8.  **★★ Soft targets at two temperatures.** For logits $2$, $0$ and $-1$, compute the softmax at temperatures $1$ and $4$, to three decimals, and both entropies, to three decimals. Compare the entropies with $\log 3$.

    *Solution*: Example 5.3. At temperature 1 the vector is 0.844, 0.114, 0.042 and the entropy is 0.524. At temperature 4 the vector is 0.481, 0.292, 0.227 and the entropy is 1.048. Both lie below $\log 3 = 1.099$, as Proposition 5.2 requires.

9.  **★★★ A false negative in a contrastive pair.** Compute the one-negative InfoNCE loss for similarities $1$ and $0$ at temperature $0.5$. Then suppose the negative is a second crop of the same tumour. Using Proposition 6.2, say which similarity descent decreases, and why a later probe for tumour against normal can suffer.

    *Solution*: The loss equals $\log(1 + e^{-2}) = 0.1269$. Descent decreases the negative similarity, so the two tumour crops are pushed apart. A linear probe must then send two distant vectors to one label. The margin of that probe can shrink because the tumour class occupies a larger region. State this mechanism. Do not invent an accuracy.

10. **★★★ A large attention weight on a zero value.** For query 1, keys 1 and 0, and values 2 and 5, with dimension 1, compute the weights and the output to four decimals. Then replace the values by 0 and $2e+5$ and show that the output is unchanged while the first weight stays large. Say what the weight fails to explain.

    *Solution*: Example 7.3 and Proposition 7.2. The weights are $0.7311$ and $0.2689$. The output is $2.8068$. The new second value is $10.4366$, and $0.2689 \times 10.4366 = 2.8068$. The first weight remains $0.7311$ and multiplies zero. The weight is not the influence of the token.

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

Enrolled students are graded on the practical session reports for 50% and on a written or oral exam for 50%. The oral option depends on the number of students. No cutoff is displayed. The Université Paris-Saclay table calls the assessment partial continuous assessment. External auditors may attend and receive no grade, no assessment and no certificate. The four subjects below are proposals for the practical reports. The written paper is a proposal for the exam. The same three questions can be asked aloud if the instructors choose the oral form. None of these proposals is the instructors' sheet.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Distilling a teacher on synthetic images, a paper study.** Read Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015) and reproduce the soft-target comparison on images you can generate on a laptop. Class 0 is a bright square and class 1 is a bright disk, on a 32 by 32 canvas, plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.3, seed 0. The teacher is a one-hidden-layer network with 128 units. The student has 32 units. Match the teacher at temperature 4, then predict at temperature 1.

    -   *Deliverables*: code, a report of 4 to 6 pages, and a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: [ch. 0](#ch0) and [ch. 5](#ch5). The entropy numbers in Example 5.3 are the check that your softmax is scaled correctly.
    -   *Success*: on a held-out set of $2000$ images, the student's divergence to the teacher's soft targets at temperature $4$ is below $0.05$, and the student has fewer than half the teacher's parameters.
    -   *Evaluation*: the practical-report rows of the rubric. The official weight of all practical reports together is 50%.

2.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] A small-scale reading of Transfusion, a paper study.** Read Raghu, Zhang, Kleinberg and Bengio (NeurIPS 2019) and reproduce their question, not their ImageNet table. The question is whether a pretrained encoder helps more when labels are scarce. Build a synthetic pretraining set and a labelled set of circles and rectangles with a corner marker that plays the role of a scanner token. Freeze the encoder. Fit a linear probe at $20$, $50$, $100$ and $400$ labels. Repeat with the marker removed at test time.

    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4-page report, and an 8-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: [ch. 1](#ch1), [ch. 2](#ch2) and [ch. 3](#ch3). Proposition 2.2 is the reason the probe training is convex.
    -   *Success*: the report plots probe accuracy against the four label counts, with and without the marker at test time, from a fixed seed. State which encoder wins at each count.
    -   *Evaluation*: the practical-report rows of the rubric.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 2-3 · ≈ 30 h each] Importance weights against a gradient-reversal encoder.** Implement Proposition 3.2 and the gradient-reversal method of Ganin and coauthors (2016) on a two-class Gaussian mixture with a mean shift between source and target, in the spirit of Ex. 6. Use a shared nonlinear feature map. Compare with a classifier trained on the source only.

    -   *Split*: one member owns the weights, one owns the adversarial head, and one owns the fixed test set and the table of risks.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 6-page report, and a 15-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: [ch. 0](#ch0) and [ch. 3](#ch3).
    -   *Success*: the report tables the target 0-1 risk of the source-only model, the weighted model and the adversarial model on one frozen test set of $5000$ points. Identify the lowest target risk.
    -   *Evaluation*: the practical-report rows of the rubric. Each member states which rows they own.

2.  **[Group of 2-3 · ≈ 30 h each] Contrastive pretraining against a tiny transformer, a paper study.** Study Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi and Hinton (2020). On synthetic $32 \times 32$ images, train a one-negative or small-batch InfoNCE encoder with crops and rotations, then a linear probe. Train a tiny patch transformer from scratch on the same labels. Include a corner marker and a test condition that removes it.

    -   *Split*: one member owns the views and the contrastive loss, one owns the transformer, and one owns the probe curves and the marker ablation.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 6-page report, and a 15-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: [ch. 6](#ch6) and [ch. 7](#ch7). Proposition 6.2 is the loss check. Proposition 7.2 is the attention check.
    -   *Success*: the report gives probe accuracy and transformer accuracy at $100$ and at $1000$ labels, seed $0$, with and without the marker at test time.
    -   *Evaluation*: the practical-report rows of the rubric.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Format: 2 hours, one handwritten sheet of notes, no computer and no phone. Three questions, 20 points. An oral exam, if chosen because of the number of students, asks the same three questions.

1.  **Conceptual question (6 points).** Define a representation. Say what a frozen linear probe is, and why its logistic loss is a convex function of its weights. A labelled set has $40$ images. A probe has about $10^3$ weights and a fine-tuned network has about $10^6$ weights. Give one reason to fit the probe first.

    *Expected*: Definition 1.1 and Proposition 2.2. The logit is affine in the probe weights and the logistic loss is convex in the logit, so a local minimum is global. The network has far more free weights than labels, so the probe is the better-posed first fit. Cite the small-set regime discussed with Raghu and coauthors (2019).

2.  **Computation (7 points).** For logits $2$, $0$ and $-1$, give the softmax at temperatures $1$ and $4$, to three decimals, and both entropies, to three decimals. Which vector is more uncertain, and what number can the entropy not exceed?

    *Expected*: Example 5.3. Temperature 1 gives 0.844, 0.114, 0.042 and entropy 0.524. Temperature 4 gives 0.481, 0.292, 0.227 and entropy 1.048. The second vector is more uncertain. Proposition 5.2 forbids an entropy above $\log 3 = 1.099$.

3.  **Short proof (7 points).** Define scaled dot-product attention for one query and several key-value pairs. Prove that the output is a convex combination of the values. Deduce that a value equal to the zero vector does not change the output.

    *Expected*: Definition 7.1 and Proposition 7.2. The exponential is positive and the weights divide by their sum, so the weights are positive and sum to $1$. The output is that weighted sum of values. A zero value adds the zero vector. The matching weight may stay large.

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

The official split is 50% practical reports and 50% written or oral exam. The rows below use that split.

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Practical report: the success table or figure comes from the fixed seed | 25% | The stated accuracy, divergence or risk is computed, not replaced by a screenshot from a paper |
| Practical report: the write-up uses the named paper and the cited chapters | 15% | The argument quotes the right proposition and does not invent a clinical number |
| Practical report: the code runs on a laptop CPU with NumPy or PyTorch | 10% | One command rebuilds the main table from the seed in the subject |
| Exam, conceptual question | 15% | Definition and convexity reason, with the comparison of $40$ labels to the two parameter counts |
| Exam, computation | 15% | Both softmax vectors, both entropies, and the comparison with $\log 3$ |
| Exam, short proof | 20% | The coefficients are non-negative and sum to $1$, and the zero-value consequence |
